L16@P0: Abstract
L17@P0: World models constitute a promising approach for training reinforcement learning
L18@P0: agents in a safe and sample-efficient manner. Recent world models predominantly
L19@P0: operate on sequences of discrete latent variables to model environment dynamics.
L20@P0: However, this compression into a compact discrete representation may ignore
L21@P0: visual details that are important for reinforcement learning. Concurrently, diffusion
L22@P0: models have become a dominant approach for image generation, challenging
L23@P0: well-established methods modeling discrete latents. Motivated by this paradigm
L24@P0: shift, we introduce DIAMOND (DIffusion As a Model Of eNvironment Dreams),
L25@P0: a reinforcement learning agent trained in a diffusion world model. We analyze
L26@P0: the key design choices that are required to make diffusion suitable for world
L27@P0: modeling, and demonstrate how improved visual details can lead to improved
L28@P0: agent performance. DIAMOND achieves a mean human normalized score of 1.46
L29@P0: on the competitive Atari 100k benchmark; a new best for agents trained entirely
L30@P0: within a world model. We further demonstrate that DIAMOND’s diffusion world
L31@P0: model can stand alone as an interactive neural game engine by training on static
L32@P0: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive gameplay. To foster future research on diffusion
L33@P0: for world modeling, we release our code, agents, videos and playable world models
L34@P0: at https://diamond-wm.github.io.
L35@P0: 1 Introduction
L36@P0: Generative models of environments, or “world models" (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018), are becoming
L37@P0: increasingly important as a component for generalist agents to plan and reason about their environment
L38@P0: (LeCun, 2022). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated a wide variety of successes in recent
L39@P0: years (Silver et al., 2016; Degrave et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022), but is well-known to be sample
L40@P0: inefficient, which limits real-world applications. World models have shown promise for training
L41@P0: reinforcement learning agents across diverse environments (Hafner et al., 2023; Schrittwieser et al.,
L42@P0: 2020), with greatly improved sample-efficiency (Ye et al., 2021), which can enable learning from
L43@P0: experience in the real world (Wu et al., 2023).
L44@P0: Recent world modeling methods (Hafner et al., 2021; Micheli et al., 2023; Robine et al., 2023;
L45@P0: Hafner et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) often model environment dynamics as a sequence of discrete
L46@P0: latent variables. Discretization of the latent space helps to avoid compounding error over multi-step
L47@P0: time horizons. However, this encoding may lose information, resulting in a loss of generality and
L48@P0: reconstruction quality. This may be problematic for more real-world scenarios where the information

L150@P1: In this case, small details in the visual input, such as a traffic light or a pedestrian in the distance,
L151@P1: may change the policy of an agent. Increasing the number of discrete latents can mitigate this lossy
L152@P1: compression, but comes with an increased computational cost (Micheli et al., 2023).
L153@P1: In the meantime, diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020) have
L154@P1: become a dominant paradigm for high-resolution image generation (Rombach et al., 2022; Podell
L155@P1: et al., 2023). This class of methods, in which the model learns to reverse a noising process, challenges
L156@P1: well-established approaches modeling discrete tokens (Esser et al., 2021; Ramesh et al., 2021; Chang
L157@P1: et al., 2023), and thereby offers a promising alternative to alleviate the need for discretization in world
L158@P1: modeling. Additionally, diffusion models are known to be easily conditionable and to flexibly model
L159@P1: complex multi-modal distributions without mode collapse. These properties are instrumental to world
L160@P1: modeling, since adherence to conditioning should allow a world model to reflect an agent’s actions
L161@P1: more closely, resulting in more reliable credit assignment, and modeling multi-modal distributions
L162@P1: should provide greater diversity of training scenarios for an agent.
L163@P1: Motivated by these characteristics, we propose DIAMOND (DIffusion As a Model Of eNvironment
L164@P1: Dreams), a reinforcement learning agent trained in a diffusion world model. Careful design choices
L165@P1: are necessary to ensure our diffusion world model is efficient and stable over long-time horizons, and
L166@P1: we provide a qualitative analysis to illustrate their importance. DIAMOND achieves a mean human
L167@P1: normalized score of 1.46 on the well-established Atari 100k benchmark; a new state of the art for
L168@P1: agents trained entirely within a world model. Additionally, operating in image space has the benefit
L169@P1: of enabling our diffusion world model to be a drop-in substitute for the environment, which provides
L170@P1: greater insight into world model and agent behaviors. In particular, we find the improved performance
L171@P1: in some games follows from better modeling of critical visual details. To further demonstrate the
L172@P1: effectiveness of our world model in isolation, we train DIAMOND’s diffusion world model on 87 hours
L173@P1: of static Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CSGO) gameplay (Pearce and Zhu, 2022) to produce an
L174@P1: interactive neural game engine for the popular in-game map, Dust II. We release our code, agents and
L175@P1: playable world models at https://diamond-wm.github.io.
L176@P1: 2 Preliminaries
L177@P1: 2.1 Reinforcement learning and world models
L178@P1: We model the environment as a standard Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP)
L179@P1: (Sutton and Barto, 2018), (S, A, O, T, R, O, γ), where S is a set of states, A is a set of discrete
L180@P1: actions, and O is a set of image observations. The transition function T : S×A×S → [0, 1] describes
L181@P1: the environment dynamics p(st+1 | st, at), and the reward function R : S × A × S → R maps
L182@P1: transitions to scalar rewards. Agents cannot directly access states st and only see the environment
L183@P1: through image observations xt ∈ O, emitted according to observation probabilities p(xt | st),
L184@P1-2: 2described by the observation function O : S × O → [0, 1]. The goal is to obtain a policy π that
L185@P2: maps observations to actions in order to maximize the expected discounted return Eπ[

L192@P2: models of environments, i.e. models of p(st+1, rt | st, at). These models can be used as simulated
L193@P2: environments to train RL agents (Sutton, 1991) in a sample-efficient manner (Wu et al., 2023). In
L194@P2: this paradigm, the training procedure typically consists of cycling through the three following steps:
L195@P2: collect data with the RL agent in the real environment; train the world model on all the collected data;
L196@P2: train the RL agent in the world model environment (commonly referred to as "in imagination").
